source: Katzung16 ch56-58; GG14 ch9; KDT8 ch68

cards.front: What is the difference between toxicokinetics and toxicodynamics?
cards.back: Toxicokinetics is the absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion of toxins or toxic doses of drugs and their metabolites; toxicodynamics is their injurious effect on body functions. Both resemble, but can differ importantly from, ordinary pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics.

cards.front: What are the common ways poisoned patients die?
cards.back: CNS depression with loss of airway reflexes and respiratory drive (airway obstruction, aspiration, apnoea: opioids, sedatives); cardiovascular toxicity (hypotension, arrhythmias); cellular hypoxia despite oxygen (cyanide, hydrogen sulfide, carbon monoxide); seizures, rigidity and hyperthermia with rhabdomyolysis; delayed organ damage (paraquat lung fibrosis, acetaminophen or mushroom liver necrosis); and trauma from behavioural effects.

cards.front: Define hazard and risk in toxicology.
cards.back: Hazard is the capacity of a chemical to cause injury in a given setting, judged from its inherent toxicity and the likely exposure; it is often a subjective estimate. Risk is the expected frequency of an undesirable effect from exposure, estimated by extrapolating dose-response data to real exposure levels.

cards.front: What is the therapeutic index and margin of safety in toxicology terms?
cards.back: Therapeutic index = LD50/ED50 in animals, or TD50/ED50 in humans (TD50 = dose toxic to 50%). Margin of safety = LD1/ED99. Low-TI drugs such as digoxin and anticancer agents need caution and drug monitoring; high-TI drugs such as penicillin are relatively safe.

cards.front: Why does volume of distribution matter in a poisoned patient? Give examples.
cards.back: A large Vd means the toxin sits in tissues and cannot be removed by blood-cleansing methods like haemodialysis. Large Vd (>5 L/kg): antidepressants, antipsychotics, antimalarials, opioids, propranolol, verapamil. Small Vd (<1 L/kg), more accessible: salicylate, acetaminophen, ethanol, phenobarbital, lithium, valproate, phenytoin.

cards.front: How does overdose alter a drug's pharmacokinetics?
cards.back: Slow tablet dissolution or gastric emptying can delay peak toxicity; a corrosive poison may increase absorption by injuring the gut wall; saturated hepatic metabolism reduces first-pass effect; saturated protein binding raises the free fraction; and saturated elimination shifts first-order to zero-order kinetics, prolonging apparent half-life.

cards.front: Case: a tablet overdose patient looks well at 1 h but deteriorates later. Using kinetics, why, and how does Vd guide whether dialysis will help?
cards.back: Overdose can slow absorption, so peak toxicity may come late. Haemodialysis helps only some poisons: Katzung lists lithium, salicylate, phenobarbital, valproate and theophylline as dialysable, and antidepressants, propranolol and opioids as not useful. Large volume of distribution (tricyclics) means little drug is in plasma to clear.

cards.front: Complete: vital-sign clues in poisoning
cards.text: Hypertension with tachycardia: {{amphetamines}}, cocaine, antimuscarinics. Hypotension with bradycardia: {{calcium channel blockers}}, beta-blockers, clonidine, sedative-hypnotics. Hypotension with tachycardia: {{tricyclic antidepressants}}, trazodone, quetiapine, vasodilators. Rapid breathing: {{salicylates}}, carbon monoxide. Hyperthermia: sympathomimetics, {{anticholinergics}}, salicylates.

cards.front: Complete: eye signs in poisoning
cards.text: Miosis: {{opioids}}, clonidine, phenothiazines, {{cholinesterase inhibitors}}. Mydriasis: amphetamines, cocaine, LSD, {{atropine}}. Horizontal nystagmus: phenytoin, alcohol, barbiturates. Vertical plus horizontal nystagmus: {{phencyclidine}}. Ptosis with ophthalmoplegia: {{botulism}}.

cards.front: Which poisons cause a raised anion gap metabolic acidosis?
cards.back: Anion gap = (Na + K) - (HCO3 + Cl), normally 12-16 mEq/L (8-12 without K). Organic acid metabolites: methanol, ethylene glycol, diethylene glycol. Lactic acidosis: cyanide, carbon monoxide, ibuprofen, isoniazid, metformin, salicylates, valproate, and any seizures, hypoxia or hypotension. Iron also causes it.

cards.front: What is the osmol gap and which poisons raise it?
cards.back: Measured minus calculated serum osmolality (calculated from Na, glucose and BUN; normal 280-290 mOsm/L). Unmeasured osmoles raise the gap: ethanol, methanol, ethylene glycol, isopropyl alcohol, acetone, propylene glycol.

cards.front: What are the limits of toxicology screening?
cards.back: Rapid urine drugs-of-abuse screens cover few drug classes and give false positives and negatives; comprehensive screens are slow and costly; many dangerous drugs (calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, isoniazid) are not detected; and a positive screen shows exposure but not time or amount. Clinical examination with routine labs usually suffices; quantitative levels (acetaminophen, salicylate, lithium, theophylline, methanol) guide antidotes or dialysis.

cards.front: What is the current status of induced emesis and gastric lavage?
cards.back: Syrup of ipecac (emetine, cephaeline) is ineffective, no longer recommended and no longer made in the USA. Gastric emptying removes only about a third of a dose even under ideal conditions; lavage risks oesophageal or gastric trauma, aspiration and vagal stimulation, so it is reserved for unusual cases on toxicologist advice and only with a protected airway.

cards.front: Classify: haemodialysis in poisoning
cards.text: Dialysis may help in poisoning with {{lithium}}, {{salicylate}}, {{methanol}} and ethylene glycol, theophylline, metformin, phenobarbital, carbamazepine and valproate. It is not useful for {{tricyclic antidepressants}}, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, calcium channel blockers, {{digoxin}}, opioids and propranolol, mainly because of large Vd.

cards.front: Which bedside clues suggest a corrosive or hydrocarbon poisoning?
cards.back: Burns around the mouth suggest a corrosive substance; a hydrocarbon odour on the breath suggests a hydrocarbon solvent. A chest radiograph may show hydrocarbon pneumonia.

cards.front: Which poisonings contraindicate induced emesis?
cards.back: Kerosene or petroleum, corrosive acids or alkalis, and CNS stimulants. Emesis is also avoided in comatose or haemodynamically unstable patients, or those with an inadequate gag reflex.

cards.front: Does activated charcoal adsorb hydrocarbons and organic solvents?
cards.back: No. Strong acids and alkalis, metallic salts, iodine, cyanide, caustics, alcohol, hydrocarbons and other organic solvents are not adsorbed by charcoal. Charcoal is also withheld in paralytic ileus or intestinal obstruction.

cards.front: Which supportive measures are used in phosphide poisoning?
cards.back: Mechanical ventilation, organ support, vasoactive drugs, and correction of electrolyte and glucose abnormalities.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: Where should phosphide-poisoned patients be managed, and why?
cards.back: In an ICU, because of the high risk of multi-organ failure and death.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: What is the first step after inhaling phosphine?
cards.back: Move the person away from the source and give supplemental oxygen if needed.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: Which national centre gives round-the-clock poisoning advice in India?
cards.back: The National Poisons Information Centre (NPIC) at AIIMS, New Delhi. It was set up in 1995 in the Department of Pharmacology.
refs: WEB AIIMS NPIC Introduction (National Poisons Information Centre) https://www.aiims.edu/index.php/en/npic_intro

cards.front: What are the NPIC helpline numbers and hours?
cards.back: Toll-free 1800 116 117; telephone 26589391 or 26593677. Open 24 hours a day, all year.
refs: WEB AIIMS NPIC Introduction (National Poisons Information Centre) https://www.aiims.edu/index.php/en/npic_intro

cards.front: What does NPIC advise when poisoning is suspected?
cards.back: Do not wait for symptoms, do not treat the person yourself, and take them to the nearest health facility.
refs: WEB AIIMS NPIC Introduction (National Poisons Information Centre) https://www.aiims.edu/index.php/en/npic_intro

cards.front: Complete: National Poisons Information Centre
cards.text: The National Poisons Information Centre was set up in {{1995}} in the Department of {{Pharmacology}} at {{AIIMS}}, New Delhi.
refs: WEB AIIMS NPIC Introduction (National Poisons Information Centre) https://www.aiims.edu/index.php/en/npic_intro

cards.front: Which drugs are listed as not removed by haemodialysis?
cards.back: Amphetamines, antidepressants, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, calcium channel blockers, digoxin, metoprolol, propranolol, opioids.

cards.front: Short note: Initial management of a poisoned patient

points: Clear vomitus; positioning or jaw thrust; oral airway or endotracheal tube
Observation, pulse oximetry, end-tidal CO2, blood gases; ventilate if insufficient
Monitor pulse, BP, urine output, perfusion; IV access and bloods
Concentrated dextrose for altered mental status unless glucose is normal
Thiamine for alcoholic or malnourished patients (prevents Wernicke)
Naloxone for suspected opioid depression
Flumazenil only for pure benzodiazepine overdose: avoid with chronic benzodiazepine use, tricyclic overdose or seizure disorder
Toxicological history and examination; decontamination alongside stabilisation

cards.front: Activated charcoal: how does it work and what does it not bind?
cards.back: Its huge porous surface adsorbs many poisons; aim for at least 10:1 charcoal to toxin by weight. It does not bind iron, lithium or potassium, binds alcohols and cyanide poorly, and is not useful for corrosive acids or alkalis. Repeated doses can enhance elimination of carbamazepine, dapsone and phenobarbital (gut dialysis) by interrupting enterohepatic cycling and drawing drug back into the gut.

cards.front: Whole bowel irrigation: what is it and when is it used?
cards.back: Oral or nasogastric iso-osmotic polyethylene glycol-electrolyte solution given until the rectal effluent is clear. Used for iron, sustained-release or enteric-coated tablets, drug packets in body packers and drug patches. Contraindicated with bowel perforation or obstruction, ileus, uncontrolled vomiting, an unprotected airway or GI bleeding.

cards.front: When is urinary pH manipulated in poisoning?
cards.back: Alkalinisation with IV sodium bicarbonate ion-traps weak acids: salicylate (first-line only for moderate poisoning not needing dialysis), phenobarbital, chlorpropamide. Acidifying urine for amphetamines or phencyclidine is not advised as it worsens renal injury from rhabdomyolysis. Forced diuresis is unproven and risks fluid overload.

cards.front: Why is gastric lavage controversial in phosphide poisoning?
cards.back: It may increase phosphine release and toxicity. Staff are also at risk, because phosphine can escape from vomit and faeces.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: What role does activated charcoal play in metal phosphide ingestion?
cards.back: It is described as beneficial for reducing toxicity. Evidence for coconut oil and potassium permanganate lavage is lacking.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: Short note: Anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) poisoning

points: Red as a beet (flushed), hot as a hare (hyperthermia), dry as a bone (no sweating)
Blind as a bat (cycloplegia), mad as a hatter (confusion, delirium); sinus tachycardia, ileus
Supportive care; benzodiazepine or antipsychotic for agitation
Physostigmine for severe peripheral or central effects, given slowly IV
Do not give physostigmine in tricyclic overdose
Antihistamines and tricyclics are common causes

cards.front: Short note: Dextrose challenge and naloxone in altered consciousness

points: Hypoglycaemia mimics intoxication
Adults 25 g IV (50 mL of 50%); children 0.5 g/kg (2 mL/kg of 25%)
Unless a bedside test shows normal glucose
0.4-2 mg IV, IM or SC for opioid poisoning
Larger doses for propoxyphene, codeine, fentanyl derivatives
Effect often shorter than the opioid; respiratory depression is the main killer

cards.front: Focal seizure or motor deficit in a poisoned patient suggests what?
cards.back: A structural lesion such as intracranial haemorrhage, not a toxic or metabolic cause.

cards.front: Essay: General principles of management of acute poisoning

points: Most deaths are intentional overdoses; prompt supportive care keeps mortality low
ABC, dextrose, thiamine, naloxone
Treat seizures, hypotension, temperature
History, toxidromes (vital signs, pupils, skin, bowel sounds, neurology)
Anion and osmol gaps, ECG (QRS, QTc), X-ray, selective drug levels
Skin and eye washing
Activated charcoal; whole bowel irrigation for selected ingestions
Lavage and ipecac rarely or never
Specific antidotes exist for only a few poisons
Haemodialysis for small-Vd toxins
Urinary alkalinisation
Multiple-dose charcoal
Child-resistant packaging, education, poison information services

cards.front: Essay: Toxidrome clues from the bedside examination

points: Hypertension and tachycardia: amphetamines, cocaine, antimuscarinics
Hypotension and bradycardia: calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, clonidine, sedative-hypnotics
Miosis: opioids, clonidine, phenothiazines, cholinesterase inhibitors
Mydriasis: amphetamines, cocaine, LSD, antimuscarinics
Sweating: organophosphates, nicotine, sympathomimetics
Ileus: antimuscarinic, opioid, sedative
Cramps and diarrhoea: organophosphates, iron, arsenic, theophylline
Nystagmus, ataxia: phenytoin, carbamazepine, alcohol

cards.front: Essay: Enhanced elimination of poisons

points: More efficient than peritoneal dialysis
Corrects fluid, electrolyte and acid-base; removes formic, oxalic and glycolic acids
Useful for carbamazepine, lithium, methanol, salicylate, theophylline, valproic acid
Peritoneal dialysis: inefficient for most drugs
Urinary alkalinisation: salicylate; acidification for phencyclidine and amphetamines
Forced diuresis: not recommended
Interrupts enterohepatic cycling and aids gut elimination
Used for carbamazepine, quinine, dapsone, salicylate

cards.front: Complete: specific antidotes
cards.text: Acetaminophen: {{acetylcysteine}}. Iron: {{deferoxamine}}. Digoxin: {{digoxin antibodies}}. Methanol and ethylene glycol: {{fomepizole}} or ethanol. Beta-blockers: {{glucagon}}. Cyanide: {{hydroxocobalamin}}. Opioids: {{naloxone}}. Benzodiazepines: {{flumazenil}}. Organophosphates: atropine plus {{pralidoxime}}. Tricyclic cardiotoxicity: {{sodium bicarbonate}}. Fluoride and calcium channel blockers: {{calcium}}. Carbon monoxide: {{oxygen}}. Theophylline/caffeine tachycardia: {{esmolol}}.

cards.front: Is there a specific antidote for phosphide poisoning?
cards.back: No. None is known, so treatment is mainly supportive, usually in an ICU.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: What is the evidence for N-acetylcysteine in phosphide poisoning?
cards.back: Used in some regimens for phosphide-related acute liver failure. A mortality benefit has not been proven.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: What is the evidence for pralidoxime in phosphide poisoning?
cards.back: Animal data only so far: rat survival rose at 10 mg/kg of aluminium phosphide. Benefit in humans has not been studied.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: When is physostigmine used as an antidote, and when must it not be used?
cards.back: For central and peripheral anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) delirium, given slowly IV with monitoring; effects last only 30-60 min. It can cause bradycardia, bronchial secretions and seizures (keep atropine ready) and must not be used in tricyclic overdose, where it can cause heart block or asystole.

cards.front: Scorpion sting: why is prazosin the drug of choice, and what warning applies to its first dose?
cards.back: Scorpion venom is neurotoxic and cardiotoxic. It can cause hypertension, which prazosin treats; severe cases also get pulmonary oedema. Early in prazosin treatment, marked postural hypotension can occur.

cards.front: Scorpion sting: which drugs control seizures, muscle spasm and hypotension from anaphylaxis?
cards.back: Diazepam for seizures; lignocaine for muscle spasm and pain; intramuscular adrenaline when anaphylaxis causes hypotension.

cards.front: Cobra and krait bite: why does paralysis occur, and what is added for cobra paralysis?
cards.back: Cobra venom is a curare-like neurotoxin that blocks nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction, causing paralysis and respiratory paralysis. Specific antivenom serum is the primary treatment. For cobra paralysis, neostigmine with atropine is added: neostigmine raises acetylcholine to overcome the block, and atropine blocks its muscarinic effects. Krait paralysis is presynaptic and is not expected to respond to edrophonium, so the regimen is for cobra.

cards.front: US rattlesnake envenomation: why should field remedies be avoided, and what is definitive treatment?
cards.back: Incision and suction, tourniquets and ice packs do more harm than good, while avoiding unnecessary movement helps limit the spread of venom. Definitive treatment is early intravenous antivenom.

cards.front: Pralidoxime: benefit in carbamate and organophosphate poisoning?
cards.back: No proven benefit in carbamate poisoning; uncertain benefit in established organophosphate poisoning.

cards.front: Case: a confused patient has dilated pupils, dry skin and wide QRS after an overdose. Is physostigmine appropriate, and which antidote class fits instead?
cards.back: Anticholinergic delirium alone would justify slow IV physostigmine, but a wide QRS suggests tricyclic overdose, where physostigmine can cause heart block or asystole and must be avoided. Tricyclic cardiotoxicity is treated with sodium bicarbonate.

cards.front: Recognise the anticholinergic toxidrome.
cards.back: Red as a beet (flushed), hot as a hare (hyperthermia), dry as a bone (no sweating), blind as a bat (mydriasis, cycloplegia), mad as a hatter (delirium), with sinus tachycardia, ileus and urinary retention. Seizures suggest an antihistamine or tricyclic. Treatment is supportive (benzodiazepine for agitation, bladder catheter), with physostigmine for marked agitation if no tricyclic is involved.

cards.front: Which common plants contain cardiac glycosides with properties similar to digoxin?
cards.back: Oleander, lily of the valley and milkweed, among others. Digoxin itself is obtained from the white foxglove (Digitalis lanata).

cards.front: How soon do features of aluminium or zinc phosphide ingestion usually start?
cards.back: Usually within about 30 minutes. Early features are nausea, vomiting and epigastric pain; garlic-like breath may occur.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: Complete: tricyclic antidepressant overdose
cards.text: Tricyclics widen the {{QRS}} complex beyond {{100 ms}}. Seizures reflect {{GABA-A}} antagonism, and dry mouth, tachycardia and dilated pupils reflect {{antimuscarinic}} action.

cards.front: Antidote preferred to ethanol in methanol or ethylene glycol poisoning?
cards.back: Fomepizole: easier to use; ethanol gives blood levels that are difficult to keep safe.

cards.front: Is haemodialysis useful for opioid overdose?
cards.back: No: opioids are listed as not removed effectively by haemodialysis. Naloxone is the antidote.

cards.front: Short note: Acetaminophen (paracetamol) poisoning

points: Acute intake above 150-200 mg/kg (children) or 7 g (adults) is potentially toxic
Early: no or mild GI symptoms
24-36 h: rising transaminases, hypoprothrombinaemia
Fulminant liver failure: acidosis, hypoglycaemia, encephalopathy, death; renal failure possible
Serum level >150 mg/L at about 4 h indicates risk; alcoholics and enzyme-induced patients at risk at lower levels
Acetylcysteine (glutathione substitute) binds the toxic metabolite; best within 8-10 h
Liver transplant for fulminant failure

cards.front: Short note: Tricyclic antidepressant overdose

points: Antimuscarinic: tachycardia, dilated pupils, dry mouth
Alpha blockade: vasodilation, hypotension
GABA-A antagonism and antihistamine action: seizures
Cardiac Na+ channel block: wide QRS, depressed contractility, ventricular arrhythmias
More than about 1 g (15-20 mg/kg) potentially lethal
Supportive care, airway, IV fluids; norepinephrine preferred for hypotension
Sodium bicarbonate bolus for wide QRS (raises extracellular Na+)
Avoid physostigmine and flumazenil

cards.front: Short note: Salicylate poisoning

points: Uncouples oxidative phosphorylation; acute intake >200 mg/kg likely toxic; chronic overmedication in the elderly
Early hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis, then raised anion gap metabolic acidosis (mixed picture)
Hyperthermia, vomiting, dehydration
Severe: seizures, coma, pulmonary oedema, collapse; enteric-coated tablets delay toxicity
Gut decontamination after massive ingestion; IV fluids
IV bicarbonate to alkalinise urine (ion trapping)
Haemodialysis for severe acidosis, coma or very high levels

cards.front: Why is propranolol the most dangerous beta-blocker in overdose, and what is the antidote?
cards.back: In overdose all beta-blockers lose selectivity; propranolol also blocks Na+ channels (like tricyclics, giving wide QRS and seizures) and is lipophilic, entering the CNS, so even 2-3 times the therapeutic dose can be serious. Fluids, beta agonists and atropine often fail; glucagon raises cardiac cAMP independent of beta-receptors.

cards.front: How is calcium channel blocker overdose managed?
cards.back: Supportive care plus early whole bowel irrigation and charcoal (most are sustained-release) before ileus sets in; IV calcium for depressed contractility; high-dose insulin with glucose, glucagon, methylene blue, veno-arterial ECMO, and lipid emulsion in case reports for severe verapamil toxicity. Verapamil and diltiazem cause bradycardia and shock; dihydropyridines cause vasodilation with reflex tachycardia, but selectivity is lost in massive overdose.

cards.front: Methanol and ethylene glycol poisoning: why toxic and how treated?
cards.back: Both cause drunkenness and an osmol gap, then a delayed severe anion gap acidosis as alcohol dehydrogenase makes toxic acids: formic acid from methanol (blindness) and oxalic and glycolic acids from ethylene glycol (renal failure; oxalate crystals in urine). Treatment: block alcohol dehydrogenase with fomepizole (or ethanol), and haemodialysis for acidosis or end-organ damage.

cards.front: Digoxin toxicity: features and treatment.
cards.back: Vomiting; hyperkalaemia in acute overdose (hypokalaemia from diuretics worsens chronic toxicity); bradycardia, AV block, atrial tachycardia with block, junctional rhythm, ventricular ectopics and bidirectional VT. Atropine for bradycardia; IV digoxin-specific antibody fragments usually help within 30-60 min and may work for other cardiac glycosides such as oleander.

cards.front: Theophylline poisoning: features and treatment.
cards.back: Tachycardia, tremor, vomiting, hypotension, hypokalaemia, hyperglycaemia (beta-2 overactivity), atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, and refractory seizures in severe cases; sustained-release forms delay toxicity. Treat with repeated charcoal, whole bowel irrigation, a beta-blocker such as esmolol for hypotension and tachycardia, and haemodialysis at very high levels or with intractable seizures.

cards.front: Short note: Organophosphate pesticide poisoning

points: Phosphorylation of the esteratic site of acetylcholinesterase; ACh accumulates
Muscarinic (DUMBELS: diarrhoea, urination, miosis, bronchospasm, lacrimation, salivation, sweating)
Nicotinic: fasciculations, weakness, respiratory paralysis, BP/heart rate changes
CNS: agitation, seizures
Protect rescuers; decontaminate
Atropine, dose doubled every 10-15 min until secretions and wheeze settle
Pralidoxime early, acts at muscarinic and nicotinic sites; outcome benefit uncertain
Intermediate syndrome: progressive neuromuscular failure, may need ventilation
Delayed polyneuropathy (OPIDP) from neuropathy target esterase inhibition; no specific treatment

cards.front: Datura (dhatura) poisoning: which plant and alkaloids are involved?
cards.back: Datura (dhatura) poisoning is a form of belladonna poisoning. The plant is a source of atropine, which is D,L-hyoscyamine. Its toxicity is anticholinergic, and physostigmine is the specific antidote.

cards.front: Why are iron-containing multivitamins a poisoning risk in young children?
cards.back: Iron is widely present in over-the-counter vitamins, and as few as 10 to 12 prenatal multivitamin tablets with iron can cause serious illness in a small child.

cards.front: Inhalant abuse: which substances are involved, and how is overdose managed?
cards.back: Recreational inhalation of nitrites, ketones, and aliphatic or aromatic hydrocarbons such as benzene and toluene. Chronic aromatic hydrocarbon exposure causes toxicity in many organs, including white-matter lesions in the CNS. Overdose management is supportive.

cards.front: Short note: Aluminium phosphide poisoning, clinical features

points: Nausea, vomiting, epigastric pain
Garlic-like breath may occur
Circulatory collapse and hypotension
Myocarditis, pericarditis, pulmonary oedema, heart failure
ECG: ST-T change and arrhythmias; echo may show reduced LV function
Acute kidney injury and jaundice
Liver injury can progress to acute liver failure; DIC is common
Inhalation: chest tightness, headache, lethargy, convulsions, delirium
Circulatory failure is the major cause of death
Hypokalaemia and hypoglycaemia are frequent
Serum magnesium may be high, low or normal

refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: Short note: Stimulant poisoning (amphetamine, cocaine, MDMA)

points: Methamphetamine, MDMA (ecstasy), cocaine (crack); pseudoephedrine and ephedrine
Hypertension, tachycardia, agitation, acute psychosis
Seizures, hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis from prolonged muscular hyperactivity
No specific antidote; supportive care
Seizures: IV benzodiazepines such as lorazepam
Severe hyperthermia is life-threatening and needs aggressive treatment

cards.front: Short note: Serotonin toxicity

points: SSRIs, especially combined with each other or with MAOIs
Agitation, muscle hyperactivity, hyperthermia
Generalised hypertonicity and lower-extremity clonus
Seizures possible

cards.front: Short note: Theophylline poisoning

points: 20-30 tablets can be fatal in an adult
Vomiting, sinus tachycardia, tremor; hypotension, hypokalaemia, hyperglycaemia
Repeated charcoal and whole bowel irrigation
Esmolol or propranolol for beta-mediated hypotension and tachycardia
Haemodialysis for severe cases

cards.front: Short note: Snake envenomation (rattlesnake)

points: Severe pain, swelling, haemorrhagic bleb, fang marks
Systemic: nausea, vomiting, fasciculations, shock, coagulopathy, low platelets
Avoid incision, suction, tourniquets and ice (more harm than good)
Limit unnecessary movement
Definitive treatment: intravenous antivenom

cards.front: Essay: Aluminium phosphide poisoning

points: Reacts with water and acid to release phosphine
Proposed: cytochrome C oxidase inhibition, mitochondrial damage, lipid peroxidation (clearer in vitro)
Onset usually within about 30 minutes
GI symptoms, circulatory collapse, myocarditis, pulmonary oedema
Acute kidney injury, jaundice, acute liver failure, DIC
Lavage is controversial; charcoal described as beneficial
No known antidote; supportive care in ICU
N-acetylcysteine used in liver failure, benefit unproven
High case fatality; about 26% of pesticide poisonings at PGI Chandigarh (1990 to 2004)

refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: Complete: chelator choice in metal poisoning
cards.text: Lead: {{calcium disodium EDTA}} or oral {{succimer}}. Acute arsenic: {{unithiol}} or dimercaprol. Acute inorganic mercury: unithiol, dimercaprol or succimer. Acute iron: {{desferrioxamine}}. Copper and Wilson disease: {{penicillamine}}. Dimercaprol is contraindicated in {{iron}} and {{cadmium}} poisoning because its complexes are toxic.

cards.front: Complete: chelators in lead and metal poisoning
cards.text: In lead poisoning the main chelator is {{CaNa2EDTA}}, and {{dimercaprol}} is added as an adjuvant in severe cases. {{Succimer}} is an oral option; penicillamine is the drug of choice for {{copper}} poisoning.

cards.front: Which chelator is used in Wilson disease and copper poisoning?
cards.back: Penicillamine, which chelates copper.

cards.front: Short note: Lead poisoning

points: Inhaled dust (industry) or ingestion; adults absorb 10-15%, young children up to 50%
About 99% of blood lead in red cells; over 90% of adult body burden in bone (half-life years)
Developing brain most sensitive; no safe threshold in children
Encephalopathy at very high levels; motor neuropathy with wrist drop
Blocks ALA dehydratase and ferrochelatase: raised zinc protoporphyrin, anaemia, basophilic stippling
Lead colic, gingival lead line
Nephropathy, saturnine gout
Hypertension, cardiovascular mortality; miscarriage, reduced sperm
Whole blood lead

cards.front: How is inorganic lead poisoning treated?
cards.back: Stop exposure and give supportive care. Encephalopathy is an emergency: treat cerebral oedema and seizures, and chelate with IV calcium disodium EDTA (some start with IM dimercaprol, then both together). Parenteral chelation is limited to 5 days, then oral succimer. Blood lead may rebound as bone lead re-equilibrates. Chelation of asymptomatic children with moderate levels did not improve cognition.

cards.front: Short note: Arsenic poisoning

points: Groundwater (Ganges delta of India and Bangladesh), wood preservatives, semiconductors, herbicides
Gastroenteritis, capillary leak, shock; QT prolongation and arrhythmias
Pancytopenia within a week; ascending sensorimotor neuropathy after 2-6 weeks; Mees lines on nails
Raindrop hyperpigmentation, palm-sole hyperkeratosis, stocking-glove neuropathy
Cancer of lung, skin and bladder; peripheral vascular disease
Urine arsenic (avoid seafood for 3 days before testing); hair and nails for past exposure
Acute: decontamination, intensive care, prompt unithiol IV or dimercaprol IM
Chronic: stop exposure; chelation unproven

cards.front: How does arsine gas poisoning differ from other arsenic poisoning?
cards.back: Arsine causes massive intravascular haemolysis after a 2-24 h latent period, with jaundice, haemoglobinuria and oliguric renal failure. Chelators are of no proven value; treatment is supportive with exchange transfusion, hydration and haemodialysis.

cards.front: Short note: Mercury poisoning

points: Inhaled; acute pneumonitis
Chronic triad: intention tremor, erethism (shyness, irritability), gingivostomatitis
Mercuric chloride: corrosive haemorrhagic gastroenteritis, then acute tubular necrosis
Minamata Bay; fish
Paraesthesias, ataxia, hearing loss, dysarthria, constricted visual fields
Teratogen: cerebral palsy-like syndrome in offspring
Painful red extremities in children with subacute or chronic exposure
Acute inorganic: early unithiol, dimercaprol or succimer, hydration, dialysis if renal failure
Avoid dimercaprol in chronic elemental or organic mercury: it redistributes mercury to the brain

cards.front: What general principles limit chelation therapy?
cards.back: Benefit falls rapidly as the time from exposure grows; metal held long in an organ (e.g. lead in bone) is removed poorly; chelators can redistribute metal to vital organs (dimercaprol moves mercury and arsenic into the brain; chelators move cadmium into the kidney); and essential metals are lost (zinc with calcium EDTA, zinc and copper with succimer).

cards.front: Short note: Dimercaprol (BAL)

points: Oily dithiol chelator; two SH groups bind arsenic, mercury and similar metals
Developed as an antidote to the arsenical war gas lewisite
Acute arsenic, inorganic mercury, gold, bismuth, nickel, antimony poisoning
Adjunct to CaNa2EDTA in severe lead poisoning
5 mg/kg IM stat, then 2-3 mg/kg every 4-8 h for 2 days
Given IM as 10% in peanut oil
Contraindicated in iron and cadmium poisoning (complexes are toxic)
Hypertension, tachycardia, vomiting; antihistamine given before reduces these

cards.front: Short note: Succimer (DMSA)

points: Water-soluble analogue of dimercaprol
Orally effective
FDA approved for children with blood lead above 45 mcg/dL
Used in arsenic and mercury poisoning; dimercaprol-like action on sulfhydryl enzymes
Typical dose 10 mg/kg orally three times a day
Nausea and anorexia; may mildly increase zinc and copper excretion

cards.front: Short note: Calcium disodium EDTA (edetate calcium disodium)

points: Calcium form protects against calcium depletion and tetany
Disodium EDTA IV bolus causes tetany
Main drug for lead poisoning
Also zinc, manganese, cadmium and some radionuclides
1 g in 200-300 mL saline or glucose, infused over 1 h, twice daily for 3-5 days
Proximal tubular necrosis; reduce with high urine flow
Febrile reaction and anaphylactoid reactions reported
Avoid in anuria; poor oral absorption, so IV only

cards.front: Short note: Penicillamine as a chelator

points: D-isomer used; a degradation product of penicillin
Chelates copper, mercury, lead and zinc
Wilson disease; drug of choice for copper poisoning
Alternative to dimercaprol or succimer for mercury
Cystinuria: soluble penicillamine-cysteine complex
Scleroderma: increases soluble collagen
Take 1 h before or 2 h after meals
Short-term use mild; long-term causes dermatological, renal, haematological and collagen toxicity

cards.front: Short note: Desferrioxamine (deferoxamine)

points: Iron-chelating agent from an actinomycete; 1 g chelates about 85 mg iron
Poorly absorbed orally; given parenterally
Acute iron poisoning, mainly in children; can be life-saving
Transfusion siderosis in thalassaemia: 0.5-1 g/day IM; or 2 g per unit of blood IV
Histamine release: hypotension, flushing, itching, urticaria
Repeated use can change lens and retina

cards.front: Short note: Deferiprone and deferasirox (oral iron chelators)

points: Oral; 50-100 mg/kg daily in 2-4 divided doses
Simplifies transfusion siderosis; less effective than injected desferrioxamine
Adverse: anorexia, vomiting, joint pain, reversible neutropenia, rarely agranulocytosis
20 mg/kg once daily on an empty stomach, tablet dispersed in water or juice
Lowers serum ferritin in transfusion overload and non-transfusion dependent thalassaemia
Dose adjusted by serum ferritin

cards.front: Why is CaNa2EDTA given IV and not orally?
cards.back: Poor oral absorption, and oral EDTA may increase lead absorption from the gut. It is given by slow infusion.

cards.front: Why is dimercaprol contraindicated in iron and cadmium poisoning?
cards.back: The dimercaprol-iron and dimercaprol-cadmium complexes are themselves toxic.

cards.front: Why is dimercaprol avoided in chronic elemental or methylmercury exposure?
cards.back: It redistributes mercury to the central nervous system.

cards.front: Why must chelation start as early as possible after an acute metal exposure?
cards.back: Metal is still in accessible pools. Metal already in slowly exchanging tissue, such as long half-life stores, is removed less effectively.

cards.front: Essay: Chelation therapy in heavy metal poisoning

points: Chelator binds metal as a ring; 5-7 membered ring most stable
Ligands are O, N or S atoms
Water-soluble complex excreted in urine
Dimercaprol: arsenic, mercury, gold; adjunct in lead
CaNa2EDTA: lead
Succimer: lead in children, oral
Penicillamine: copper, Wilson disease
Desferrioxamine, deferiprone, deferasirox: iron
Efficacy falls as time from exposure increases
Redistribution to other organs (dimercaprol)
Depletes zinc and copper (EDTA, succimer, penicillamine)

cards.front: Name classic environmental chemical disasters and their toxins.
cards.back: Bhopal, India (1984): methyl isocyanate, almost 4000 deaths and over half a million injured. Minamata, Japan: methylmercury in seafood. Itai-itai disease, Japan: cadmium in water. Seveso, Italy (1976): dioxin. Yusho (Japan) and Yucheng (Taiwan): PCB-contaminated cooking oil.

cards.front: Why is carbon monoxide dangerous even when inspired oxygen is normal?
cards.back: CO binds haemoglobin about 220 times more avidly than oxygen and also impairs release of O2 from the remaining haemoglobin, so tissues are starved while PO2 and pulse oximetry can look normal.

cards.front: Which enzyme does cyanide inhibit and what is the hallmark result?
cards.back: Cyanide binds ferric iron of cytochrome oxidase, so cells cannot use oxygen: lactic acidosis with high venous oxygen content, seizures, coma and collapse.

cards.front: Antidote for carbon monoxide poisoning?
cards.back: 100% oxygen, which cuts the CO half-time from about 320 min on room air to about 80 min; hyperbaric oxygen shortens it further.

cards.front: Carbon monoxide poisoning: mechanism, features and treatment.
cards.back: CO binds haemoglobin about 220 times more avidly than oxygen and impairs O2 release from the remaining haemoglobin. Headache and malaise at lower carboxyhaemoglobin, syncope around 40%, death above 60%. Pulse oximetry and PO2 can be falsely normal. Give 100% oxygen: CO half-time falls from about 320 min on room air to about 80 min; hyperbaric oxygen shortens it further and is favoured in pregnancy.

cards.front: Cyanide poisoning: mechanism and antidotes.
cards.back: Cyanide binds ferric iron of cytochrome oxidase, blocking cellular oxygen use: lactic acidosis, seizures, coma and collapse, with high venous O2 content. Sources: fires (plastics, wool), cassava, fruit seeds. Antidotes: hydroxocobalamin (forms cyanocobalamin), or sodium nitrite (methaemoglobin binds cyanide) with sodium thiosulfate (helps rhodanese form thiocyanate).

cards.front: Short note: Air pollutants and their health effects

points: Highly soluble: forms sulfurous acid in the upper airway
Bronchoconstriction, bronchorrhoea; asthmatics very sensitive
Poorly soluble deep-lung irritant: pulmonary oedema, ARDS
Silo-filler's disease; late bronchiolitis obliterans
Ground-level ozone from NOx and organic compounds in sunlight
Free-radical injury, airway hyperresponsiveness, pulmonary oedema at high levels
PM10 deposits in upper airways; PM2.5 reaches gas-exchange areas
Worsens asthma and COPD; linked to cardiovascular mortality
No specific antidote: supportive airway care, reduce outdoor exposure, masks and air filtration

cards.front: Differentiate bioaccumulation and biomagnification.
cards.back: Bioaccumulation: a persistent chemical builds up in an organism when intake exceeds metabolism and excretion (e.g. organochlorines in body fat). Biomagnification: concentration rises at each step up the food chain; PCBs in the Great Lakes rose almost 50,000-fold from phytoplankton to herring gulls.

cards.front: Halogenated hydrocarbon solvents (carbon tetrachloride, chloroform, trichloroethylene): which organs do they injure, and is there a specific treatment?
cards.back: They depress the CNS and damage the liver and kidney (cardiotoxicity is seen in animals), and several are probable human carcinogens. There is no specific treatment, so management follows the organ involved.

cards.front: Why does cyanide cause lactic acidosis even when oxygen is available?
cards.back: Cyanide binds cytochrome oxidase in mitochondria, so cells cannot use oxygen. They switch to anaerobic metabolism and produce lactate.

cards.front: Short note: Cyanide poisoning and antidotes

points: Binds ferric iron of cytochrome oxidase
Cellular hypoxia despite normal oxygen tension
Shortness of breath, agitation, tachycardia, then seizures, coma, hypotension
Hydroxocobalamin (Cyanokit) 5 g IV over 15 min; converts cyanide to cyanocobalamin
Conventional kit: nitrite (methaemoglobin binds cyanide) plus thiosulfate (to thiocyanate)
Binds cyanide poorly; may reduce absorption

cards.front: Short note: Irritant gases (chlorine, ammonia, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides)

points: Corrosive effect on upper and lower airways
Cough, stridor, wheezing, pneumonia
Humidified oxygen
Bronchodilators
Supportive care

cards.front: Compare carbon monoxide and cyanide: both block oxygen delivery or use, so how do mechanism, bedside clues and antidotes differ?
cards.back: CO: binds haemoglobin, reduces O2 carriage and release; pulse oximetry and PO2 misleading; treat with 100% (or hyperbaric) oxygen. Cyanide: binds cytochrome oxidase so O2 is not used; lactic acidosis with high venous O2; treat with hydroxocobalamin, or sodium nitrite (methaemoglobin traps cyanide) plus sodium thiosulfate (rhodanese forms thiocyanate). Both cause cellular hypoxia, a major route to death in poisoning.

cards.front: What share of pesticide poisonings at PGI Chandigarh (1990 to 2004) was aluminium phosphide?
cards.back: About 26%. It had the highest case fatality of the agents studied there.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: Complete: phosphide chemistry
cards.text: Aluminium and zinc phosphides release {{phosphine}} gas when they react with {{water}} and {{acid}}.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: Are fungicides and weedicides covered by the Insecticides Act?
cards.back: Yes, if the Central Government adds them to the schedule after consulting the Central Insecticides Board.
refs: WEB Govt of India Insecticides Act 1968 (Act 46 of 1968) https://development.delhi.gov.in/sites/default/files/development/pdf_files/the_insecticidesact-1968.pdf

cards.front: Which body advises governments on technical matters under the Insecticides Act?
cards.back: The Central Insecticides Board, which advises both Central and State governments.
refs: WEB Govt of India Insecticides Act 1968 (Act 46 of 1968) https://development.delhi.gov.in/sites/default/files/development/pdf_files/the_insecticidesact-1968.pdf

cards.front: What must happen before an insecticide is imported or manufactured?
cards.back: It must be registered. Apply to the Registration Committee, with a separate application for each insecticide. Registration can be refused if the claimed precautions cannot control a serious risk.
refs: WEB Govt of India Insecticides Act 1968 (Act 46 of 1968) https://development.delhi.gov.in/sites/default/files/development/pdf_files/the_insecticidesact-1968.pdf

cards.front: Who grants licences to sell, stock or distribute insecticides?
cards.back: A licensing officer appointed by the State Government.
refs: WEB Govt of India Insecticides Act 1968 (Act 46 of 1968) https://development.delhi.gov.in/sites/default/files/development/pdf_files/the_insecticidesact-1968.pdf

cards.front: Who can inspect insecticide stock and take samples?
cards.back: Insecticide Inspectors, appointed by the Central or a State Government. A sample is divided into three sealed portions.
refs: WEB Govt of India Insecticides Act 1968 (Act 46 of 1968) https://development.delhi.gov.in/sites/default/files/development/pdf_files/the_insecticidesact-1968.pdf

cards.front: How long can an insecticide be banned while its risk is investigated?
cards.back: Up to 60 days, extendable by up to 30 days in total if the investigation is unfinished.
refs: WEB Govt of India Insecticides Act 1968 (Act 46 of 1968) https://development.delhi.gov.in/sites/default/files/development/pdf_files/the_insecticidesact-1968.pdf

cards.front: Penalty for a first offence of importing or manufacturing an insecticide without a registration certificate?
cards.back: Imprisonment up to two years, or a fine up to Rs 2,000, or both (as printed in the Act).
refs: WEB Govt of India Insecticides Act 1968 (Act 46 of 1968) https://development.delhi.gov.in/sites/default/files/development/pdf_files/the_insecticidesact-1968.pdf

cards.front: Penalty for a first breach of the Act's other provisions, such as a registration or licence condition?
cards.back: Imprisonment up to six months, or a fine, or both.
refs: WEB Govt of India Insecticides Act 1968 (Act 46 of 1968) https://development.delhi.gov.in/sites/default/files/development/pdf_files/the_insecticidesact-1968.pdf

cards.front: Is ignorance of an insecticide's risk a defence in a prosecution under the Act?
cards.back: No, except for the exceptions the Act provides.
refs: WEB Govt of India Insecticides Act 1968 (Act 46 of 1968) https://development.delhi.gov.in/sites/default/files/development/pdf_files/the_insecticidesact-1968.pdf

cards.front: Complete: Insecticides Act
cards.text: Insecticides must be {{registered}} before import or manufacture; selling them needs a {{licence}}; the {{Central Insecticides Board}} advises on technical matters.
refs: WEB Govt of India Insecticides Act 1968 (Act 46 of 1968) https://development.delhi.gov.in/sites/default/files/development/pdf_files/the_insecticidesact-1968.pdf

cards.front: Organochlorine pesticides: groups, mechanism and toxicity.
cards.back: Groups: DDT and analogues, benzene hexachlorides, cyclodienes, toxaphenes. They delay sodium channel inactivation, causing repetitive neuronal firing and CNS stimulation: tremor (DDT) or convulsions first. No specific treatment. They persist, bioaccumulate in fat and act as endocrine disrupters, so most are banned.

cards.front: How do carbamate pesticides differ from organophosphates?
cards.back: Carbamates carbamoylate the cholinesterase esteratic site; binding is weaker and reverses within minutes to hours, so poisoning is shorter and the enzyme recovers spontaneously faster. Organophosphates bind more lastingly but are not persistent in the environment (hydrolysis and photolysis), unlike organochlorines.

cards.front: Short note: Paraquat poisoning

points: Single-electron reduction to free radicals; probably inhibits superoxide dismutase
Actively concentrated in the lung
Early haematemesis and bloody stools
Days later: haemorrhagic pulmonary oedema, then progressive fibrosis; liver, kidney, heart involvement; death after weeks
Bind early with adsorbents (Fuller's earth, activated charcoal); no gastric lavage
Use oxygen cautiously as it worsens lung injury
Steroids, cyclophosphamide, antioxidants of unproven value; high fatality

cards.front: Glyphosate herbicide poisoning: features.
cards.back: Common in suicidal ingestions in developing countries. Eye and skin irritant; ingestion causes oesophageal erosion, aspiration pneumonia and renal failure, partly due to the surfactant in formulations. Treatment is symptomatic (dialysis for renal failure). IARC lists glyphosate as probably carcinogenic (2A), with an association with non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

cards.front: Pyrethroid insecticides: toxicity and treatment.
cards.back: Mainly irritant and allergic: eye, skin and airway irritation, irritant asthma, rarely anaphylaxis, and cutaneous paraesthesias in sprayers; severe exposures can cause convulsions. Treatment is symptomatic; ivermectin, pentobarbital and mephenesin have been used.

cards.front: Polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs): why a concern?
cards.back: Stable, lipophilic, poorly metabolised industrial chemicals that bioaccumulate (food, especially fish, is the main source). Exposure causes chloracne and other skin changes, liver abnormalities and raised triglycerides; they are endocrine disrupters, prenatal exposure is linked to cognitive deficits, and some are IARC class 1 carcinogens.

cards.front: Why are perfluoro compounds (PFAS, such as PFOA) a concern?
cards.back: They are persistent, accumulate in humans and wildlife, and spread through water and the food chain. PFOA has an estimated human half-life of about 3 years, and it acts as an endocrine disruptor.

cards.front: Aluminium and zinc phosphide: which toxic gas do they release, and what speeds the reaction?
cards.back: Phosphine gas. Phosphides react with water and acid to release it, and acid makes the reaction much faster.
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: Zinc phosphide poisoning: what mortality range is reported?
refs: WEB NCBI-PMC Rodenticide Poisoning (D'Silva and Krishna, Indian J Crit Care Med) 2019 https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6996659/

cards.front: Insecticides Act 1968: what is its main purpose?
cards.back: To regulate import, manufacture, sale, transport, distribution and use of insecticides, to prevent risk to humans or animals.
refs: WEB Govt of India Insecticides Act 1968 (Act 46 of 1968) https://development.delhi.gov.in/sites/default/files/development/pdf_files/the_insecticidesact-1968.pdf

cards.front: Short note: Insecticides Act 1968, key provisions

points: Regulate import, manufacture, sale, transport, distribution and use
Prevent risk to humans and animals
Central Insecticides Board advises governments
Registration Committee registers insecticides
State licensing officers and Insecticide Inspectors
Each insecticide needs its own registration application
Sale, stock or distribution needs a licence
Government may ban sale or use for up to 60 days pending investigation
First offence of the main kind: up to 2 years, or fine up to Rs 2,000, or both
Other breaches: up to 6 months, or fine, or both

refs: WEB Govt of India Insecticides Act 1968 (Act 46 of 1968) https://development.delhi.gov.in/sites/default/files/development/pdf_files/the_insecticidesact-1968.pdf

cards.front: Compare organophosphate, carbamate, organochlorine and pyrethroid pesticide toxicity: mechanism, duration and treatment.
cards.back: Organophosphates and carbamates inhibit cholinesterase; carbamate binding is weaker and reverses within minutes to hours, OPs bind more lastingly (atropine plus pralidoxime for OP; pralidoxime has no proven benefit in carbamates). Organochlorines delay sodium channel inactivation giving CNS stimulation and convulsions, persist in fat, are endocrine disrupters and have no specific treatment. Pyrethroids are mainly irritant and allergic, treated symptomatically.

cards.front: What is ecotoxicology?
cards.back: The study of how chemical pollutants harm populations, communities and ecosystems, and how those agents move through the environment. Traditional toxicology focuses on single organisms.

cards.front: What are PPCPs in environmental toxicology?
cards.back: Pharmaceutical and personal care products. Together with industrial and chemical pollutants they are often non-degradable and survive stomach acid, so they persist and spread through excreta, water and the food chain.

cards.front: Define bioaccumulation and biomagnification.
cards.back: Bioaccumulation: a persistent agent builds up in an organism's tissue (e.g. body fat) because it is released slowly. Biomagnification: its concentration rises at each step up the food chain, so animals near the top, including humans, carry the highest load.

cards.front: Essay: Adverse impact of drugs in the ecosystem and preventive measures

points: Ecotoxicology covers effects on populations and ecosystems, not only individuals
Drugs and their metabolites reach the environment after use and disposal
Excretion of unchanged drug and metabolites into sewage
Flushing unused or expired drugs down toilets and sinks
Direct discharge of manufacturing effluent; sludge spread on land and leaching
Persistence and re-entry into water supplies and the food chain
Chronic toxicity and microbial resistance; disruption of microbial ecosystems
Endocrine disruption, growth inhibition, cytotoxicity, mutagenicity and teratogenicity in animals, plants and humans
Bioaccumulation in fat, then biomagnification up the food chain
Strict regulation of safe disposal of unused drugs
Controlled waste routes: incineration, landfill, immobilisation
Effluent control at manufacturing sites and monitoring after a drug is launched
Reduce exposure to persistent chemicals; risk assessment links exposure limits to laws

cards.front: Short note: Biomagnification of persistent pollutants

points: Rising concentration of a persistent agent at each higher trophic level
Slow release from body fat keeps the agent in tissue
Persistent organochlorines accumulate in fat and are released over time
Humans, near the top of the food chain, receive the highest exposure
Chronic effects reported include endocrine disruption and carcinogenesis

cards.front: Name two common routes by which drug residues reach water.
cards.back: Unused or expired drugs flushed down toilets and sinks, and direct release of manufacturing wastewater. Excreted drug and metabolites also reach sewage.

cards.front: What is an endocrine-disrupting chemical (EDC)?
cards.back: An agent that interferes with the endocrine system by altering hormone production, transport, stability, receptor binding or signalling. It can affect reproduction, development, cognition and metabolism.

cards.front: Give examples of environmental EDCs.
cards.back: DDT and its metabolite DDE, PCBs, brominated flame retardants, phthalates, bisphenol A, and perfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). Plant phytoestrogens and mycoestrogens also act on hormone pathways.

cards.front: Short note: DDT as an endocrine disruptor

points: Efficacy, low volatility and lipid solubility; slow degradation
Metabolite DDE persists in humans and in the food chain
Some EDCs have been banned, DDT among them
Restricted use for domestic mosquito control in malaria areas of Africa

cards.front: What reproductive effects are linked to bisphenol A?
cards.back: Men exposed to BPA show lower daily sperm production, sperm count and motility. Women of reproductive age with higher BPA show a shorter luteal phase. Associations with diabetes and thyroid dysfunction are correlational, and the studies are limited.

cards.front: Why can EDC dose-response curves be U-shaped?
cards.back: Hormones and some endocrine disruptors, like essential metals, cause adverse effects at low doses, homeostasis at intermediate doses, and adverse effects again at high doses. So the dose-response is not a simple sigmoid.

cards.front: Essay: Impact of endocrine disrupters on public health and strategies to overcome it

points: EDCs mimic, enhance or block hormone actions
Found in plastics, consumer products, pesticides and food
Bind or alter hormone receptors and their downstream signalling
Alter hormone production, secretion, transport or stability; epigenetic change
Reproductive effects, such as lower sperm quality and altered luteal phase
Effects on development, cognition and metabolism
Thyroid dysfunction; links to breast and reproductive cancers are suggested, not proven
Reduce exposure, as prudence dictates for endocrine-disrupting environmental chemicals
Ban persistent agents such as DDT; prioritise and screen chemicals
Use animal studies alongside in vitro assays, which are unreliable alone for regulation
Integrate epidemiology and toxicology in risk assessment to set safe exposure limits

cards.front: What is the Ames test?
cards.back: A bacterial assay that tests whether a drug causes genetic damage (mutagenicity).

cards.front: Name the three systems used to test mutagenicity.
cards.back: Bacteria (Ames test), mammalian cell cultures, and intact rodents.

cards.front: What is an in vitro model in toxicology?
cards.back: A test system made of cells or tissues outside the intact organism, such as bacterial or mammalian cell cultures or stem-cell-derived organoids.

cards.front: Short note: Stem-cell-derived organoids in toxicity testing

points: Three-dimensional organoids made from human pluripotent stem cells
In vitro assays alone are unreliable for regulatory purposes

cards.front: Why are animal studies still needed alongside in vitro assays?
cards.back: In vitro assays alone are unreliable for regulation, so animal studies are considered indispensable. Long-term whole-life rodent studies, under GLP, detect carcinogenicity.

cards.front: Essay: In vitro model systems in toxicology

points: In vitro systems test toxicity outside the intact organism
Toxicologists use lab studies to examine mechanisms and predict harm
Bacterial assays (Ames test) for mutagenicity
Mammalian cell cultures
Stem-cell-derived three-dimensional organoids
Screening for genetic damage before whole-animal testing
Mechanistic study of toxic effects
Unreliable alone for regulatory purposes
Animal studies, including long-term carcinogenicity tests under GLP, are indispensable

cards.front: Which reactive oxygen species arise in toxicology, and what do they damage?
cards.back: Superoxide (O2-), produced in uncoupled CYP reactions, and hydroxyl radicals. They attack lipids, proteins and macromolecules, especially in biological membranes.

cards.front: What does superoxide dismutase do?
cards.back: It is an endogenous enzyme that converts superoxide, limiting its toxic effects.

cards.front: Name the endogenous enzymes that scavenge toxic oxygen by-products.
cards.back: Superoxide dismutase, glutathione peroxidase and catalase.

cards.front: Which endogenous reducing agents limit oxygen toxicity?
cards.back: Glutathione and ascorbate.

cards.front: Why does oxygen toxicity still occur despite endogenous defences?
cards.back: The defences are insufficient against high oxygen concentrations over an extended period, so toxicity still occurs.

cards.front: Short note: Glutathione and paracetamol toxicity

points: Reactive metabolite NAPQI is detoxified by conjugation with glutathione
Glucuronidation saturates, more NAPQI forms, hepatic glutathione is depleted
NAPQI then binds covalently to liver (and renal tubular) proteins

cards.front: How do endogenous enzymes protect against anthracycline toxicity?
cards.back: Superoxide dismutase and catalase counter the free radicals that anthracyclines generate, especially with iron. Exogenous antioxidants such as alpha-tocopherol, or the iron chelator dexrazoxane, can augment this protection.

cards.front: Essay: Endogenous antioxidants

points: Oxygen metabolism produces reactive oxygen species
Oxidative stress damages lipids, proteins and membranes
Superoxide dismutase converts superoxide
Glutathione peroxidase and catalase scavenge toxic by-products
Glutathione and ascorbate act as reducing agents
Paracetamol: glutathione depletion by NAPQI
Anthracyclines: SOD and catalase protect against radicals
Defences fail under high oxygen for long periods
Exogenous antioxidants can augment protection

cards.front: What is saturated (zero-order) elimination in overdose?
cards.back: Once a metabolic or excretory pathway is saturated, a fixed amount is cleared per unit time; ethanol at high intake is the classic example.

cards.front: Why can a modified-release overdose look benign early and then turn toxic?
cards.back: Modified-release forms and drugs that slow gastric emptying delay the peak concentration, so symptoms appear late; observation must cover the expected peak time.

cards.front: Short note: Toxicokinetics and toxicodynamics in drug overdose

points: Toxicokinetics: pharmacokinetics of a drug under toxic exposure; data mostly case reports and observational studies
Toxicodynamics: concentration-effect relation, including non-monotonic dose-response curves
Modified-release forms and slow gastric emptying delay the peak
Large acetaminophen ingestions can give two peaks 12 to 42 h apart
Protein binding saturates, raising the free fraction
Acidosis lowers tricyclic protein binding and increases toxicity
Large volume of distribution: poorly removed by haemodialysis
Saturated pathways become zero order (ethanol; phenytoin at high levels)
Shunting to toxic pathways: acetaminophen to NAPQI, glutathione depletion
Active metabolites can be more potent (tramadol to M1)
Time to peak sets the observation period
Kinetic data guide decontamination and choice of enhanced elimination

cards.front: Which calcium channel blocker class causes vasodilatory hypotension with reflex tachycardia in overdose?
cards.back: Dihydropyridines (for example nifedipine and amlodipine), which act mainly on vascular channels.

cards.front: Which calcium channel blockers cause bradycardia and cardiogenic shock in overdose, and why are they more dangerous?
cards.back: Verapamil and diltiazem: they depress sinus node automaticity, slow AV conduction and reduce cardiac output.

cards.front: What early decontamination suits sustained-release calcium channel blocker overdose?
cards.back: Whole bowel irrigation plus oral activated charcoal as soon as possible, before calcium-antagonist ileus sets in.

cards.front: Calcium in calcium channel blocker poisoning: dose and where it helps most?
cards.back: Intravenous calcium 2 to 10 g; it helps depressed contractility more than nodal block or peripheral vascular collapse.

cards.front: High-dose insulin in calcium channel blocker poisoning: dose and essential co-treatment?
cards.back: Insulin 0.5 to 1 unit/kg/h for hypotension, with glucose to maintain euglycaemia.

cards.front: Essay: Clinical toxicity, common agents and calcium channel blocker toxicity

points: Clinical toxicology studies undesired drug effects in humans and the effects and treatment of poisoning
A poison is any substance whose exposure causes a damaging physiological effect
Pharmaceuticals and illicit drugs
Plants and botanicals
Chemicals and pollutants
Calcium channel blockers cause serious toxicity with relatively small overdoses
Depress sinus node automaticity and slow AV conduction; reduce cardiac output and BP
Verapamil and diltiazem: bradycardia, hypotension, cardiogenic shock
Dihydropyridines: vasodilation, hypotension, reflex tachycardia
Massive overdose loses selectivity; all cardiovascular effects possible
